title: Measuring Integrated Information: Comparison of Candidate Measures in Theory and Simulation
authors: Pedro A. M. Mediano, Anil K. Seth, Adam B. Barrett

findings.claim: Six candidate integrated-information measures disagree with each other even on small simulated networks.
findings.quote: We find a striking diversity in the behaviour of these measures—no two measures show consistent agreement across all analyses.

quantities.condition: largest networks simulated in the comparison

findings.bears_on: Statistical integration measures are not settled or scalable enough to serve as an enforceable cap; NCI should keep its operational definition (novel bits read per block) rather than adopt one.

title: From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0
authors: Masafumi Oizumi, Larissa Albantakis, Giulio Tononi

findings.claim: IIT 3.0 evaluates integration across the minimum information partition.
findings.quote: integrated information is evaluated across the minimum information partition (MIP), the partition that makes the least difference to the cause and effect repertoires
findings.bears_on: The MIP is the closest analogue to NCI's best-case (prover-chosen) block partition; finding it is exponential in system size, whereas NCI makes the prover supply the partition as a witness.

findings.claim: Purely feed-forward systems have zero integrated information even when functionally equivalent to integrated ones.
findings.quote: there can be true “zombies” – unconscious feed-forward systems that are functionally equivalent to conscious complexes.
findings.bears_on: Loosely parallels NCI letting feed-forward inference pass while recurrent accumulation (training) is throttled; but IIT's verdict depends on the implementing structure, while NCI quantifies over every circuit computing the committed function.

title: A measure for brain complexity: relating functional segregation and integration in the nervous system
authors: Giulio Tononi, Olaf Sporns, Gerald M. Edelman

findings.claim: Neural complexity measures integration as the deviation from statistical independence of large subsets, and segregation as the independence of small subsets.
findings.quote: We express functional segregation within a neural system in terms of the relative statistical independence of small subsets of the system and functional integration in terms of significant deviations from independence of large subsets.
findings.bears_on: Integration in TSE is statistical dependence across subsets; NCI instead measures the novel bits that must cross block boundaries of one specific computation, which is checkable.

findings.claim: Complexity is high only when segregation and integration coexist, and low when parts are fully independent or fully dependent.
findings.quote: CN is shown to be high when functional segregation coexists with integration and to be low when the components of a system are either completely independent (segregated) or completely dependent (integrated).
findings.bears_on: Unlike CN, NCI is monotone: more cross-block novel information is always worse for the prover, so NCI does not reward or penalize a mix of segregation and integration.

title: An information integration theory of consciousness

findings.claim: Phi is the effective information across a system's weakest bipartition.
findings.quote: Φ is the amount of causally effective information that can be integrated across the informational weakest link of a subset of elements.
findings.bears_on: Phi minimizes information over partitions, as NCI asks whether some partition into blocks keeps each block's novel input below K; but Phi is a property of a system's dynamics, NCI of a committed circuit and a witness partition.

title: Unified Scaling Laws for Compressed Representations
authors: Andrei Panferov, Alexandra Volkova, Ionut-Vlad Modoranu, Vage Egiazarian, Mher Safaryan, Dan Alistarh

findings.claim: Compressed pretraining follows Loss = A (N rho(R))^-alpha + B D^-beta + E, where rho(R) is the representation's capacity. Under this form a compressed run at compute C reaches the loss of a full-precision run at compute rho * C (substitute N' = rho N), so the FLOP-equivalent multiplier is m = rho at every compute budget and allocation.
findings.quote: Through extensive experimentation, we identify this law to be of the form Loss(N, D) ∼ A · (N · ρ(R))−α + B · D−β + E,
findings.bears_on: The cleanest model of m(b_w, b_a): a single capacity number per representation, compute-independent, so the 1e25 value equals the small-scale fit if the form holds.

findings.claim: Fitted capacity for independent weight x activation quantization (rows weights, columns activations at 1/2/3/4/16 bits): W1 0.09/0.15/0.19/0.20/0.21; W2 0.15/0.30/0.40/0.45/0.45; W3 0.19/0.42/0.62/0.70/0.74; W4 0.20/0.46/0.72/0.85/0.90; W16 0.21/0.48/0.76/0.91/1.00.
findings.quote: Figure 6: Representation capacity coefficients for independent quantization of weights and activations. Element-wise ρ fitting error is not greater than 5 · 10−3 .
findings.bears_on: Central grid for m(b_w, b_a): 4-bit weights and activations cost 15% of compute, 2-bit 70%, 1-bit 91%; ternary (1.58) is not measured and interpolates to about 0.35 for weights alone.

findings.claim: The fits use 30M-200M models at 100 tokens per parameter, with a per-layer uniform quantizer and the QuEST gradient estimator, 1 to 8 bits, on weights, activations or both.
findings.quote: For quantization we employ the gradient estimator of [25], a per-layer uniform quantizer with static scaling factors and gradient masking. Quantization levels range from 1-bit to 8-bit precision. We consider configurations with quantized weights only, activations only, and both simultaneously.
findings.bears_on: Every cell of the grid is a 200M-parameter measurement; the 1e25 value rests on m being scale-free, which Chen and Sun's additive laws dispute.

findings.claim: Capacities of weight quantization, weight sparsity and activation quantization multiply, except in the extreme 2-bit regime where the product misfits (rho <~ 0.1).
findings.quote: Our results indicate that the representation capacity with weight sparsity sw and quantization bitwidth qw , and activation sparsity qa follows ρ(Rqw ,sw ,qa ) = ρ(Rqw ) · ρ(Rsw ) · ρ(Rqa ).

quantities.unit: absolute error of the product approximation (order)

findings.bears_on: Lets m(b_w, b_a) be written as m_w(b_w) * m_a(b_a) away from 2 bits; at 2 bits and below the measured matrix, not the product, is the estimate.

title: Scaling Laws for Floating-Point Quantization Training
authors: Xingwu Sun, Shuaipeng Li, Ruobing Xie, Weidong Han, Kan Wu, Zhen Yang, Yixing Li, An Wang, Shuai Li, Jinbao Xue, Yu Cheng, Yangyu Tao, Zhanhui Kang, Chengzhong Xu, Di Wang, Jie Jiang

findings.claim: Floating-point quantized training follows L = n/N^alpha + d/D^beta + eps + (D^beta/N^alpha) * log2(B) / (gamma (E+0.5)^delta (M+0.5)^nu) with n = 69.2343, alpha = 0.2368, d = 68973.0621, beta = 0.5162, eps = 1.9061, gamma = 11334.5197, delta = 3.1926, nu = 2.9543 (E exponent bits, M mantissa bits, B scaling block size), fitted on 366 runs at 41M-679M parameters and 10B-100B tokens.
findings.quote: The last factor could be regarded as the additional negative impact deriving from low precision training,
findings.location: Sec. 4.1 (Eq. 26 and Table 2 in the appendix); Sec. 3.2 for the 366 runs

quantities.condition: Table 2; the penalty grows as D^0.5162 / N^0.2368

quantities.unit: FLOP-equivalent multiplier m (BF16 compute to reach the same loss / compressed-run compute)
quantities.condition: derived: FP4 E2M1 weights, B = 128, C = 1e25 FLOP, N/D re-optimized, against the same law with no penalty; extrapolated (fit <= 679M x 100B); 0.81 at 1e21, 0.28 at 1e27

quantities.unit: FLOP-equivalent multiplier m (BF16 compute to reach the same loss / compressed-run compute)
quantities.condition: derived: FP8 E4M3 weights, B = 128, C = 1e25 FLOP; extrapolated

findings.bears_on: A second additive law in which FP4 weights lose a growing share of compute with scale (half at 1e25) while FP8 stays lossless.

findings.claim: The law's quantized tensors are the forward weight, the backward weight and the stored activation for the weight gradient (P2, P4, P6); forward activations and output gradients stay in high precision because quantizing them (P1, P3, P5) cost much more loss.
findings.quote: To balance efficiency and effectiveness, we’ve selected P2, P4, and P6 for quantization.

quantities.condition: quantizing P5 (dY2, the gradient input to the weight-gradient GEMM) at FP3, 'up to 2%'

findings.bears_on: Maps to the b_a = 16 column only: the law says nothing about compressing forward activations or the activation gradients that cross block boundaries.

findings.claim: Low-precision training has a critical data size past which more tokens raise the loss: for a 1B model 1730T tokens in BF16, 27T in FP8 E4M3 and 0.4T in FP4 E2M1.
findings.quote: Conversely, when the same model is trained with FP8-E4M3, the Dcrit value swiftly diminishes to 27T, and with FP4-E2M1, it further plummets to 0.4T.
findings.bears_on: Caps the over-training an FP4-weight attacker can use: a small FP4 model cannot buy back its capacity loss with more data.

title: Optimus-CC: Efficient Large NLP Model Training with 3D Parallelism Aware Communication Compression
authors: Jaeyong Song, Jinkyu Yim, Jaewon Jung, Hongsun Jang, Hyung-Jin Kim, Youngsok Kim, Jinho Lee

findings.claim: Low-rank (rank-16, about 10x) compression of the activation gradients sent backward between pipeline stages leaves GPT-8.3B and GPT-2.5B validation perplexity unchanged after 230K iterations on 128 GPUs.
findings.quote: For both the 8.3B and 2.5B models, CB and CB+FE show comparable accuracy on the baseline (no compression) model.
findings.location: evaluation, Table 2 (8.3B: 8.10 baseline, 8.10 CB; 2.5B: 9.31, 9.31) and its discussion

quantities.condition: rank-16 PowerSGD-style compression of backward inter-stage activation gradients, epilogue-only; forward activations uncompressed
GPT-8.3B, compressed backpropagation vs baseline, 230K iterations

findings.bears_on: Backward pipeline-boundary traffic tolerates ~10x compression at 8B scale with m ~ 1, but only in the partial form described in the next finding.

findings.claim: The compression applies only to the epilogue (the backward inter-stage sends on the critical path, not hidden by compute), because compressing all backward inter-stage traffic diverged; forward traffic is not compressed.
findings.quote: Epilogue-only compression was applied to all the cases because CB without epilogue-only compression diverged.
findings.bears_on: There is no at-scale evidence that every block boundary's activation gradient can be compressed ~10x without loss: the full version diverged; b_a for the backward boundary stays near 16 bits for most of the traffic.

findings.claim: Low-rank compression of the forward activations sent between pipeline stages diverged even at a very low compression rate, with the same lazy error propagation that made the backward compression work.
findings.quote: However, in our experiments, compressing the forward inter-stage activation yielded divergence in the model, even with a very low compression rate.
findings.location: lazy error propagation analysis, after Eqs. 13-14

quantities.condition: forward inter-stage activations, left uncompressed after compression diverged; GPT-2.5B/8.3B setting

findings.bears_on: The forward pipeline boundary had m = 0 (divergence) under low-rank compression; no at-scale method in this source lowers forward b_a below 16 bits at a pipeline boundary.

title: FP8-LM: Training FP8 Large Language Models
authors: Houwen Peng, Kan Wu, Yixuan Wei, Guoshuai Zhao, Yuxiang Yang, Ze Liu, Yifan Xiong, Ziyue Yang, Bolin Ni, Jingcheng Hu, Ruihang Li, Miaosen Zhang, Chen Li, Jia Ning, Ruizhe Wang, Zheng Zhang, Shuguang Liu, Joe Chau, Han Hu, Peng Cheng

findings.claim: FP8 mixed-precision pretraining (FP8 GEMMs, gradients, first Adam moment and communication) tracks the BF16 loss curve at 7B and 13B (100B tokens) and 175B (40B tokens) with unchanged hyper-parameters.
findings.quote: As shown in Fig. 4, the loss curves almost overlap with each other. The results unequivocally demonstrate that the proposed FP8 mixed-precision scheme can achieve equivalent performance to the prevalent higher-precision BF16 scheme

quantities.condition: FP8 activations and activation communication, GPT-175B, 40B tokens

quantities.unit: FLOP-equivalent multiplier m (BF16 compute to reach the same loss / compressed-run compute)
quantities.condition: derived: overlapping loss curves at equal tokens, GPT-7B/13B/175B

findings.bears_on: Pins m(8, 8) = 1 at scale: the 8-bit row and column of the grid cost nothing.

findings.claim: FP8 training still keeps master weights in FP16 with tensor scaling (or FP32) and the second Adam moment in 16 bits, because weight updates can be too small or large for 8 bits.
findings.quote: In the implementation, the master weights have two viable options: utilizing either FP32 full-precision or FP16 with tensor scaling.
findings.bears_on: Even at 8 bits the update path reads 16-bit weights; low-precision training lowers forward b_w, not the update read.

findings.claim: FP8-LM runs the sequence/tensor-parallel boundary g (forward all-gather of activations, backward reduce-scatter of activation-gradients) in FP8; the forward reduce-scatter of partial sums (g-bar) is not stated as FP8.
findings.quote: g is all-gather in forward pass and reduce-scatter in backward pass, while g¯ is reduce-scatter in forward pass and all-gather in backward pass. The gather-reduce operation g between sequence parallel and tensor parallel is executed utilizing FP8 low-precision activation, thus saving half communication costs.

quantities.condition: TP/SP boundary g in FP8 with per-tensor scaling: forward all-gathered activations and backward reduce-scattered activation-gradient partial sums; GPT 7B and 13B on 100B tokens, 175B on 40B tokens; loss curves overlap BF16

findings.bears_on: 8-bit TP boundary traffic at 7-175B, but the forward partial-sum reduction stays in high precision.

title: Towards Fully FP8 GEMM LLM Training at Scale
authors: Alejandro Hernández-Cano, Dhia Garbaya, Imanol Schlag, Martin Jaggi

findings.claim: With every GEMM inside the transformer blocks in FP8, attention included, forward and backward, the FOG architectures match the BF16 Llama3 loss at 8B parameters on 20B tokens and at 1.5B on 125B tokens (continued to 450B), while running 35-43% faster.
findings.quote: Finally, we scale the model size to 8B and train for 20B tokens. We show the divergence of other architectures with FP8DPA while FOG variants converge and match the baseline Llama3 BF16 loss, while being 35-43% faster.

quantities.condition: FP8 inputs to every GEMM in the block, attention included, forward and backward (delayed scaling)

quantities.unit: FLOP-equivalent multiplier m (BF16 compute to reach the same loss / compressed-run compute)
quantities.condition: derived: equal loss at equal tokens, 8B / 20B tokens and 1.5B / 125B tokens

findings.bears_on: Pins m(8, 8) = 1 at 8B, including the attention GEMMs that Kumar-style laws leave at 16 bits.

findings.claim: The same FP8 recipe diverges on the standard architectures (Llama3, OLMo2, OP, SmoothSwiGLU) at 390M, 1.5B and 8B; m(8, 8) = 1 needs an outlier-guarded architecture.
findings.quote: This experiment displays the unsuitability of existing architectures for FP8DPA training, as all of them diverge.

quantities.condition: largest scale at which the standard Llama3 architecture diverged with FP8 attention

findings.bears_on: Low-rate training is an architecture choice, not a drop-in: the attacker's circuit differs from the reference beyond its number formats, which the containment check must allow for.

title: Training Neural Networks from Scratch with Parallel Low-Rank Adapters
authors: Minyoung Huh, Brian Cheung, Jeremy Bernstein, Phillip Isola, Pulkit Agrawal

findings.claim: Training from scratch with parallel low-rank adapters merged into the weights (LTE) matches standard training but needs 40% more training samples to converge than data-parallel training on 8 GPUs.
findings.quote: Although our method extends the training samples required for convergence by 40%, we can fit models that are 3× bigger with roughly half the bandwidth.

quantities.unit: FLOP-equivalent multiplier m (BF16 compute to reach the same loss / compressed-run compute)
quantities.condition: derived: 1 / 1.4, same model and per-sample compute

findings.bears_on: The one compute-equivalent figure for low-rank weight updates in from-scratch training: m ~ 0.7 at vision scale, for updates that cross a node boundary at low rank.
